hints: Remember TB is a bacterial disease of the lungs - think about the genus of rod-shaped bacteria with a waxy wall that causes this specific lung infection.
walkthrough:
Recall the TB bacterium**
TB is caused by a bacterium, not a virus. The human form is Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and the cattle form that can also infect humans is Mycobacterium bovis. Either name earns the mark, with correct genus capitalised and species lower case.
Final answer: Mycobacterium tuberculosis or Mycobacterium bovis.

hints: Start from where the pathogen lives - TB mainly infects the lungs and airways, so think how microbes in the lungs could get out into the air.
Now complete the journey - how do those airborne particles move from an infected person to enter the body of an uninfected person, and why must you mention both people?
walkthrough:
Exit from infected person**
Because TB bacteria are in the lungs, coughing, sneezing, talking and breathing expel them in tiny airborne droplets of mucus and saliva.

Entry to uninfected person**
A nearby uninfected person inhales those droplets into their own lungs. You need both sides of the story - out of infected and into uninfected - for full marks.
Final answer: Airborne droplets breathed / sneezed out by an infected person and breathed in / inhaled by an uninfected person.

hints: Start inside the macrophage in Fig. 5.1 - after engulfing, what fuses with the phagosome and what happens to the bacteria inside?
Think about what the macrophage does next with the broken pieces - how does it alert other immune cells?
Consider which lymphocytes can recognise that displayed material and what makes their recognition so specific.
Once the right lymphocyte is selected, what happens to its cell numbers to build a large army quickly?
Finish the story to antibodies - which cells mature to actually secrete antibody, and which helper cells release signals to drive this?
walkthrough:
Digestion inside the macrophage**
After engulfing by phagocytosis, lysosomes fuse with the vesicle containing bacteria. Their hydrolytic enzymes hydrolyse bacterial wall components, proteins, lipids and nucleic acids. This is intracellular digestion.

Becoming an antigen-presenting cell**
The macrophage does not just destroy. It processes fragments - antigens - and displays them on its cell surface membrane. It is now an antigen-presenting cell, a signal flag for lymphocytes.

Specific recognition and clonal selection**
B-lymphocytes have antibody molecules as surface receptors and T-lymphocytes have specific receptors. Only the lymphocyte with a receptor complementary to the TB antigen binds it. This is clonal selection based on specificity.

Clonal expansion**
The selected lymphocyte divides rapidly by mitosis to form a clone of identical cells. This proliferation builds enough cells to fight the infection.

Antibody production**
B-lymphocytes mature into plasma cells which secrete large amounts of specific antibody. T-helper cells help by releasing cytokines that stimulate the B-lymphocyte humoral response.

Final answer: Lysosomes fuse with phagosome releasing hydrolytic enzymes for intracellular digestion of bacteria; antigens processed and presented on macrophage cell surface membrane so macrophage becomes antigen-presenting cell; complementary B- and T-lymphocytes selected by clonal selection; selected clones proliferate by mitosis in clonal expansion; B-lymphocytes mature to plasma cells secreting antibodies, stimulated by cytokines from T-helper cells.

hints: Think about what is left behind long after vaccination and the first response fades - which long-lived cells remain?
Compare the second meeting with the pathogen to the first - what is different about speed and strength?
Link that speed to outcome - why does faster antibody production mean the person does not become ill?
walkthrough:
Long-lived memory pool**
Vaccination leaves B and T memory cells that survive in the body for years, often a lifetime. There are many more of these specific cells than there were naive lymphocytes before.

Faster secondary response**
If the real TB bacterium enters later, these memory cells recognise it immediately. They activate faster and in greater numbers than in the primary response, so antibody concentration rises more quickly and to a higher level.

Protection before disease**
Because the response is so rapid, bacteria are destroyed before they can multiply enough to cause symptoms. That is long-term immunity.

Final answer: B and T memory cells remain for a long time; on re-infection they give a faster, larger secondary response with quicker production of higher concentration of antibodies, so pathogen destroyed before symptoms appear.

hints: Think about where TB bacteria hide in the body - if they live inside host cells, how useful are antibodies floating in plasma?
Consider whether every person in the world actually receives BCG and whether it works equally well everywhere.
Link coverage to population protection - what happens if there is no herd immunity and infected travellers move between countries?
walkthrough:
Hiding inside cells**
Mycobacterium tuberculosis is largely an intracellular parasite. Antibodies in plasma and tissue fluid cannot cross cell surface membranes to reach bacteria inside macrophages and lung cells, so humoral immunity alone cannot clear it.

Patchy and variable protection**
BCG is not part of the vaccination programme in many countries, and its effectiveness varies geographically and is low in adults. Some people do not respond well. So protection is incomplete.

No eradication without herd immunity**
Without high global coverage there is no herd immunity to stop spread. Travel, migration and collapse of health services in areas of civil disturbance allow infected people to transmit TB to non-immune populations.

Final answer: Any three from: Mycobacterium lives inside host cells where antibodies cannot reach, only effective in plasma / tissue fluid; BCG not in vaccination programme in many countries so no global herd immunity; BCG not very effective in adults / varies in effectiveness worldwide; disruption of health services / movement of infected people spreads TB.
